{{nihongo|'''Kōtai Jingū'''|皇大神宮|1=Kōtai Jingū|2=ja|3=皇大神宮|4=zh|5=皇大神宮}} is a sub Shrine of [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Jingu]]. It is officially called Kotai Jingu and colloquially called {{nihongo|'''Naikū'''|内宮|lit, inner shrine|}} and it is dedicated to [[Amaterasu]]<ref name=":0" />. [[Yata no Kagami]] is kept inside Kotai Jingu.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=[Mie] Ise Grand Shrine（伊勢神宮） |url=https://dishes-japan.com/area-guide/ise-grand-shrine/ |access-date=2023-05-05 |website=Dishes Japan |language=ja}}</ref>
When going on a pilgrimage to Ise Jingu people will typically go to the nearby {{ill|Toyōke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|1=Toyōke Daijingū|2=ja|3=豊受大神宮|4=zh|5=豐受大神宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyōke Daijingū|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyōke Daijingū|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} first and this shrine second.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Geeraert |first=Amélie |date=2021-04-07 |title=The Correct Manners When Visiting the Japanese Grand Shrine of Ise |url=https://kokoro-jp.com/culture/2236/ |access-date=2023-05-05 |website=Kokoro Media |language=en-US}}</ref>
The shrine is considered the holiest site of Shinto<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ise Jingu - Japan's Holiest Shinto Shrine |url=https://www.kanpai-japan.com/ise/jingu |access-date=2023-05-04 |website=www.kanpai-japan.com |language=en}}</ref>
The grounds of Naikū are extensive and contain a number of structures<ref name=":0">The official Ise Jingu homepage: Naiku, {{cite web |title=Isejingu |url=http://www.isejingu.or.jp/english/naigu/naigu.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/2012.06.29-183132/http://www.isejingu.or.jp/english/naigu/naigu.htm |archive-date=2012-06-29 |access-date=2008-01-09}}</ref>
== Overview ==
{{GeoGroup}}
'''{{ill|Toyōke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|4=zh|5=豐受大神宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyōke Daijingū|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} (Geku)''' and this shrine together form the core of {{ill|Ise faith|ja|伊勢信仰|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ise faith|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 伊勢神宮}}. The {{ill|Jingū taima|en|Jingū taima|qid=Q11589469|lt=Jingu Taima|1=Jingū taima}}, an amulet distributed at shrines across Japan, originates from this shrine.
When a {{ill|Shinnō|ja|親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinnō|qq=}} gets married, it is customary for them to visit the shrine as part of their honeymoon in a ceremony known as "Jingu ni essuru no gi" (神宮に謁するの儀). When visiting multiple shrines, it is common practice to start with the higher-Ranking shrine before proceeding to lower-Ranking ones. However, regular {{ill|Shinji|ja|神事|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinji|1=Shinto ritual|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11588671}} at Jingu follows the order of {{ill|Toyōke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|1=Toyōke Daijingū|2=ja|3=豊受大神宮|4=zh|5=豐受大神宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyōke Daijingū|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyōke Daijingū|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} (Geku) first, followed by the Inner Shrine (Naiku).<ref name="sk">Shikinaisha Kenkyūkai (1990): p.150</ref> This practice is referred to as '''Geku-sen-sai''' (外宮先祭).<ref name="sk"/> The correct order for pilgrims is also said to be Geku first, then Naiku.<ref>Ise Bunka-sha (2009): p.98</ref> However, for the {{ill|Jingū Shikinen Sengū|lt=Jingū Shikinen Sengū|lt=Shikinen Sengu|ja|神宮式年遷宮|1=Jingū Shikinen Sengū|1=Jingū Shikinen Sengū|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shikinen Sengu|qq=}}, the {{ill|Sengu|ja|遷御|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sengu|1=Sengyo|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q24892914}} (transfer of the deity) is performed first at Koutaijingu, then at {{ill|Toyōke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|1=Toyōke Daijingū|2=ja|3=豊受大神宮|4=zh|5=豐受大神宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyōke Daijingū|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyōke Daijingū|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}.<ref>Shikinaisha Kenkyūkai (1990): p.150</ref> Similarly, {{ill|Hōhei|ja|奉幣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hōhei|qq=}} (offering of cloth and treasures) follows the order of Toyōke Daijingū first, then Koutaijingu.
As for Betsugu (auxiliary shrines), within the grounds of Koutaijingu, there are {{ill|Aramatsuri-no-Miya|ja|荒祭宮|fr|Aramatsuri_no_miya|es|Aramatsuri no miya|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Aramatsuri-no-Miya|qq=}} and {{ill|Kazahinomi-no-Miya|ja|風日祈宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kazahinomi-no-Miya|qq=}}. Outside the main precincts, additional shrines include {{ill|Tsukiyomi-no-Miya (Naikū)|ja|月讀宮|lt=Tsukiyomi-no-Miya|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukiyomi-no-Miya (Naikū)|qq=}}, {{ill|Takihara-no-Miya|ja|瀧原宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takihara-no-Miya|qq=}}, and {{ill|Izawa-no-miya|en|Izawa-no-miya|qid=Q10885171|lt=Izawa-no-Miya|1=Izawa-no-miya}}. There are also 27 shrines (33 enshrinements) designated as Sessha (subordinate shrines), 16 shrines (16 enshrinements) designated as Massha (affiliated shrines), and 30 shrines (30 enshrinements) designated as Shokansha (administered shrines).
The architecture of the shrine, like Toyōke Daijingū, is enclosed by four layers of fences: Itakaki (板垣), Sototamagaki (外玉垣), Uchi-Tamagaki (内玉垣), and Mizugaki (瑞垣). The shrine has guard stations at the north and south gates, and Shinto priests take turns guarding and managing the premises 24/7.<ref>'General Public Restricted Areas,' History Mystery Research Association, Saizu Publishing, 2011</ref>
The nearest station is {{ill|Isuzugawa Station|en|Isuzugawa Station|qid=Q6089533|lt=Isuzugawa Station|1=Isuzugawa Station}} on the {{ill|Kintetsu Toba Line|ja|Toba Line|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kintetsu Toba Line|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Access to Ise Jingu|url=https://www.isejingu.or.jp/access/|website=Ise Jingu|access-date=2023-09-06|language=ja}}</ref> The shrine's monzenmachi (temple town) {{ill|Oharaimachi|ja|おはらい町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Oharaimachi|1=Oharaimachi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11262271}}, including {{ill|Okage Yokocho|ja|おかげ横丁|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okage Yokocho|1=Okage Yokochō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11261371}}, is one of {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|qid=Q328067|lt=Ise, Mie|1=Ise, Mie}}'s most famous {{ill|Tourist attraction|en|Tourist attraction|qid=Q570116|lt=Tourist attractions in Japan|1=Tourist attraction}}.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Travel and tourism to Ise-Shima - Okage Yokocho|url=https://okageyokocho.com/main/|website=Okage Yokocho|access-date=2023-09-06|language=ja}}</ref>
== Enshrined Deities ==
[[File:Naiku 001.jpg|thumb|right|250px|Main Shrine (October 2013)<br />The torii visible in the center is called "Itakaki South Gate," the fences on either side are called "Itakaki," the building beyond the torii is the "Outer Tamagaki South Gate"<ref name="rr28">Publishing Business Headquarters Domestic Information Division Third Editorial Department (2014): p.28</ref>, and the stone steps in the foreground are known as "Ishikikai."<ref name="gk56">Gakken Publishing (2013): p.56</ref>.]]
; Main Deity
* '''[[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Omikami]]''' (天照坐皇大御神, Amaterasu-ōmikami)
:: Worshipped as the primary deity, {{ill|Yata no Kagami|en|Yata no Kagami|qid=Q2610017|lt=Yata no Kagami|1=Yata no Kagami}}, one of the {{ill|Imperial Regalia of Japan|en|Imperial Regalia of Japan|qid=Q327465|lt=Three Sacred Treasures|1=Imperial Regalia of Japan}}, is revered as its sacred object.<ref group="note">It is generally believed that the Yata no Kagami is housed in this shrine, though other theories exist (see {{ill|Yata no Kagami|en|Yata no Kagami|qid=Q2610017|lt=Yata no Kagami|1=Yata no Kagami}}).</ref>
; Auxiliary Deities
* '''{{ill|Ame-no-Tajikarao|en|Ame-no-Tajikarao|qid=Q849412|lt=Ame-no-Tajikarao no Kami|1=Ame-no-Tajikarao}}''' (天手力男神)
:: Enshrined on the left side.<ref name="as28">Mitsuhashi (2013): p.128</ref> The {{ill|Yumi|en|Yumi|qid=Q918499|lt=Yumi|1=Yumi}} is worshipped as its sacred object.<ref name="as28"/>
* '''[[Takuhadachiji-hime|Yorozuhata Toyoakitsuhime no Mikoto]]''' (万幡豊秋津姫命)
:: Enshrined on the right side.<ref name="as28">Mitsuhashi (2013): p.128</ref> The {{ill|Sword|ja|剣|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sword|1=Double-edged sword|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11396047}} is worshipped as its sacred object.<ref name="as28"/>
== History ==
According to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|en|Nihon Shoki|qid=Q813935|lt=Nihon Shoki|1=Nihon Shoki}}, Amaterasu Ōmikami was originally enshrined in the Imperial Palace. However, in the 6th year of Emperor Sujin's reign, she was moved to {{ill|Kasanuimura|ja|笠縫邑|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasanuimura|qq=}} and enshrined by {{ill|Toyosukiiri-hime|ja|豊鍬入姫命|Toyosukiiri-hime=Toyosukiiri-hime|lt=Toyosukiiri-hime no Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyosukiiri-hime|qq=}}. In the 25th year of Emperor Suinin’s reign, {{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto|en|Yamatohime-no-mikoto|qid=Q4388732|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto|1=Yamatohime-no-mikoto}} succeeded her and traveled across the land searching for a suitable site to enshrine Amaterasu Ōmikami as her caretaker.
Although the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|en|Nihon Shoki|qid=Q813935|lt=Nihon Shoki|1=Nihon Shoki}} provides limited details of this journey, the {{ill|Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|ja|倭姫命世記|1=Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamatohime no Mikoto Seiki|qq=}}, a text believed to have been compiled in the early {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|qid=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}, describes it in great detail. The temporary sites where Amaterasu Ōmikami was enshrined along the way are known as {{ill|Moto-Ise Shrines|ja|元伊勢|1=Moto-Ise Shrines|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|13=User:Immanuelle/Moto-Ise Shrines|qq=}}. In the 26th year of Emperor Suinin’s reign, when Yamatohime no Mikoto reached {{ill|Ise Province|en|Ise Province|qid=Q864166|lt=Ise Province|1=Ise Province}}, Amaterasu Ōmikami gave an oracle stating:
"This land of divine winds, Ise, is a land where the eternal waves of Tokoyo return. It is an admirable land neighboring other provinces. I desire to dwell in this land."
Yamatohime no Mikoto then built a shrine upstream of the {{ill|Isuzu River|en|Isuzu River|qid=Q6089522|lt=Isuzu River|1=Isuzu River}}, referred to as "Iso-no-miya," marking the origin of {{ill|Kōtai Jingū|ja|皇大神宮|1=Kōtai Jingū|2=ja|3=皇大神宮|4=zh|5=皇大神宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtai Jingū|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtai Jingū|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. Due to frequent flooding in Ise, which caused the expansion of lowland areas, the shrine was constructed on a river terrace less prone to water damage.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://datazoo.jp/w/%E4%BC%8A%E5%8B%A2%E7%A5%9E%E5%AE%AE/27227327|title=Ise Jingu on TV|work=TV Detazou|date=2016-06|accessdate=2016-07-09|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160709044438/http://datazoo.jp/w/%E4%BC%8A%E5%8B%A2%E7%A5%9E%E5%AE%AE/27227327|archivedate=2016-07-09}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://news.mynavi.jp/news/2016/06/03/186/|title=Tamori and crew thrilled by the secrets of the "strongest power spot" Ise Jingu|work=Mynavi News|date=2016-06-03|accessdate=2016-07-09|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160709044950/http://news.mynavi.jp/news/2016/06/03/186/|archivedate=2016-07-09}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.sponichi.co.jp/entertainment/news/2016/06/04/kiji/K20160604012712300.html|title=Buratomori visits Ise Jingu for the first time since the Shikinen Sengu!|date=2016-06-04|accessdate=2016-07-09|publisher=Sponichi|archiveurl=https://archive.is/tr8nh|archivedate=2016-07-09}}</ref>.
Until the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji period|1=Meiji era}}, Buddhist monks were prohibited from approaching the main shrine and were required to pray from a designated "Monk's Worship Area" across the river. The renowned poet {{ill|Saigyō|en|Saigyō|qid=Q224689|lt=Saigyō|1=Saigyō}} is said to have prayed at this location and was deeply moved to tears.<ref>Kodansha (2011): p.48</ref> The {{ill|Arakida clan|ja|荒木田氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Arakida clan|qq=}} traditionally served as shrine priests, but hereditary priesthood was abolished after the Meiji Restoration.
On July 29, 1945, during the {{ill|Ujiyamada Air Raid|ja|宇治山田空襲|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ujiyamada Air Raid|qq=}}, Ujiyamada City suffered extensive damage.<ref>Ise City Compilation (1968): pp.444-445</ref> Around 40 American aircraft targeted the shrine precincts. As their aim became more precise, firebombs appeared to be drawn away towards the opposite bank of the Isuzu River instead of hitting the shrine grounds.<ref name="ss84">Yano (2006): p.184</ref> This "miracle" left the shrine unharmed, and the shrine priests were moved to tears, attributing it to the divine protection of Amaterasu Ōmikami.<ref name="ss84"/> After World War II, women of former imperial lineage have served as the shrine’s successive {{ill|Saishu (Ise Shrine)|ja|祭主|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saishu (Ise Shrine)|qq=}} (Supreme Priestess).
[[File:Ise Meisho Zue painted by Hatsusaburō Yoshida.jpg|center|thumb|867x867px|{{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|qid=Q328067|lt=Ise|1=Ise, Mie}} Meisho Zue, by Hatsusaburo Yoshida (1919)]]
== Shrine Grounds ==
[[File:Uji-bashi 06.jpg|thumb|270px|Uji Bridge (April 2010)]]
[[File:Naiku Map in Japanese.png|thumb|270px|Map of Naiku shrine grounds]]
[[File:Ise Jingu Naiku Mikakiuchi, Mishikichi West Side Version.png|thumb|270px|Inner precincts of Naiku]]
Inside {{ill|Uji Bridge (Ise City)|ja|宇治橋_(伊勢市)|lt=Uji Bridge|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Uji Bridge (Ise City)|qq=}}, aside from the main sanctuary (正宮, Shogu), are the auxiliary shrines of {{ill|Aramatsuri-no-Miya|ja|荒祭宮|fr|Aramatsuri_no_miya|es|Aramatsuri no miya|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Aramatsuri-no-Miya|qq=}} and {{ill|Kazahinomi-no-Miya|ja|風日祈宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kazahinomi-no-Miya|qq=}}. The overseer shrines include {{ill|Takimatsuri-no-Kami|ja|滝祭神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takimatsuri-no-Kami|qq=}} (Takimatsuri no Kami), {{ill|Misakadono-no-Kami|ja|御酒殿神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Misakadono-no-Kami|qq=}} (Misakadono no Kami), which enshrines the deity of sake<ref name="Uji Bridge">Ise Bunka-sha (2009), p.100</ref>, {{ill|Mishine-no-Mikura|ja|御稲御倉|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mishine-no-Mikura|qq=}}, and {{ill|Yuki-no-Mikura|ja|由貴御倉|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yuki-no-Mikura|qq=}}, which was historically used to store offerings for divine meals<ref name="Uji Bridge"/>. Additionally, {{ill|Miyanomeguri-no-Kami|ja|四至神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Miyanomeguri-no-Kami|qq=}} (Miya-no-Meguri-no-Kami), guardian deities of the shrine precincts, are also enshrined here.<ref name="Uji Bridge"/>
To the east of Uji Bridge are the overseer shrines of {{ill|Ōyamazumi Shrine (Ise)|ja|大山祇神社 (伊勢市)|lt=Ōyamazumi Shrine|lt_ja=大山祇神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōyamazumi Shrine (Ise)|qq=}} and {{ill|Koyasu Shrine (Ise)|ja|子安神社_(伊勢市)|lt=Koyasu Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Koyasu Shrine (Ise)|qq=}}. On a hill nearby is the Jingu Administrative Office (神宮司庁), which handles shrine affairs, including rituals and administration.
The shrine precincts are about ten times the size of {{ill|Toyōke Daijingū|ja|外宮|Toyōke Daijingū=Toyōke Daijingū|lt=Geku (Toyōke Daijingū)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyōke Daijingū|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 豊受大神宮}}, and unlike Geku, visitors walk on the right side of the paths.<ref>Yano (2006): pp.46-47</ref> Within the grounds are the Imibiyaden (忌火屋殿), where sacred food offerings are prepared, the Miniechousha (御贄調舎), where food is ritually prepared for the main sanctuary, the Geheiden (外幣殿), which stores sacred treasures, and the Gojoden (五丈殿), used for remote worship of auxiliary shrines. Additionally, the Saikan (斎館) is where shrine priests and officials undergo purification, while the Anzaisho (行在所) serves as an imperial lodging. Sacred horses offered by the imperial family are housed in the inner and outer stables, Uchino-miumaya (内御厩) and Sotono-miumaya (外御厩), respectively.
At the Kaguraden (神楽殿), private prayers and kagura performances are conducted, and worshippers can partake in a ritual feast at the Kyozensho (饗膳所) after making offerings. The Jingu Office for amulets and talismans distributes {{ill|Ofuda|en|Ofuda|qid=Q2500908|lt=O-fuda|1=Ofuda}}, {{ill|Omamori|en|Omamori|qid=Q1756788|lt=Omamori|1=Omamori}}, {{ill|Jingū calendar|lt=Jingū calendar|lt=Jingū calendar|ja|神宮暦|lt=Jingū calendars|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jingū calendar|qq=}}, and {{ill|Shuin|en|Shuin|qid=Q7504772|lt=Goshuin|1=Shuin}}. Visitors can also rest at the Sanshuden (参集殿), where tea and commemorative pilgrimage items are available.
The main sanctuary is located atop a stone staircase{{#tag:ref|Known as "Sekkai" (石階)<ref name="gk56"/> and constructed from Sanbaseki stone from {{ill|Gunma Prefecture|en|Gunma Prefecture|qid=Q129499|lt=Gunma Prefecture|1=Gunma Prefecture}}.<ref name="mr52">Mirai Publishing (2013), p.52</ref>|group="note"}}. Photography is only permitted up to the base of the stairs.<ref name="mr52"/> At the base of the stairs, the Miniechousha (御贄調舎) is used for the ritual preparation of abalone offerings.<ref name="mr53">Mirai Publishing (2013), p.53</ref> Ascending the stone steps, visitors enter through the Itakaki South Gate (板垣南御門), which is surrounded by a wooden fence known as Itakaki. To the east of the steps, on a stone-paved area, stands {{ill|Okitama-no-Kami|ja|屋乃波比伎神|Okitama-no-Kami=Okitama-no-Kami|lt=Yano-Hahiki-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okitama-no-Kami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 興玉神}}, who protects the sacred grounds.<ref name="gk56"/><ref>Ise Bunka-sha (2008), p.114</ref>
The area within the Itakaki is called Mikakiuchi (御垣内)<ref name="rr28"/>, covering an area of 6,807 square meters.<ref name="as16">Mitsuhashi (2013), p.16</ref> The inner sanctum housing Amaterasu Ōmikami is enclosed by three additional fences: the Outer Tamagaki (外玉垣), the Inner Tamagaki (内玉垣), and the Mizugaki (瑞垣). General visitors worship at the Outer Tamagaki South Gate (外玉垣南御門), where a white silk curtain, Mitobari (御幌), hangs.<ref name="rr28"/><ref name="mr53"/> The prescribed form of worship is "two bows, two claps, one bow."<ref name="mr53"/>
Within the Outer Tamagaki, between it and the Inner Tamagaki, stands the Nakae Torii (中重鳥居), decorated with sacred Yaesakaki (八重榊). To the east of this, the Shijo-den (四丈殿) is used for inspecting ritual offerings.<ref name="as16"/> Inside the Mizugaki fence lies the most sacred area, the Inner Sanctuary (内院), where the Main Hall (御正殿) stands.<ref name="gk35">Gakken Publishing (2013), p.56</ref> The Main Hall is built in the "Yuiitsu Shinmei-zukuri" architectural style, a form of {{ill|Shinmei-zukuri|en|Shinmei-zukuri|qid=Q930545|lt=Shinmei-zukuri|1=Shinmei-zukuri}} unique to Ise Jingu. Behind the Main Hall, the Toho-den (東宝殿) and Saiho-den (西宝殿) store sacred offerings and divine treasures.<ref name="gk35"/> At the northwest corner of the precincts, two guardian deities, {{ill|Okitama-no-Kami|ja|興玉神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okitama-no-Kami|qq=}} (Okitama-no-Kami) and {{ill|Okitama-no-Kami|ja|宮比神|Okitama-no-Kami=Okitama-no-Kami|lt=Miyabi-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okitama-no-Kami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 興玉神}} (Miyabi-no-Kami), are enshrined on a stone-paved platform.<ref>Ise Bunka-sha (2008), p.113</ref>
<gallery>
Ise-Shrine Naiku-Ujibashi-Torii.jpg|Torii and Uji Bridge (September 2023)
IseShrine.jpg|Kaguraden (July 2005)
Jingu Shicho (Jingu Administration Office).jpg|Jingu Administration Office (August 2011)
</gallery>
=== The Uji Bridge ===
[[File:Ise_Shrine_Uji-bashi1.jpg|left|thumb|The Uji Bridge, 2012]]
This 100 meter wooden bridge, built in a traditional Japanese style, stretches across the [[Isuzu River]] at the entrance of Naikū. Like the shrine buildings of Naikū, it is rebuilt every 20 years as a part of the Shikinen Sengū ceremony. The bridge is typically built by carpenters with less experience to gain more skills before moving on to take on the task of working on the main shrine.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Adams|first=Cassandra|date=Sep 1998|title=Japan's Ise Shrine and Its Thirteen-Hundred-Year-Old Reconstruction Tradition|journal=Journal of Architectural Education|volume=52|pages=49–60|doi=10.1111/j.1531-314X.1998.tb00255.x|via=JSTOR}}</ref> On crossing the bridge, the path turns to the right along the banks of the Isuzu river and passes through large landscaped gardens.
=== Temizusha ===
After crossing a short, wide bridge, pilgrims to the shrine encounter the {{ill|Chōzuya|en|Chōzuya|qid=Q1069667|lt=Temizusha|1=Chōzuya}}, a small, roofed structure containing a pool of water for use in ritual purification. Visitors are encouraged to wash their hands and rinse their mouths at Temizusha as a symbolic act to clean the mind and body of impurity. The first of two large torii gates stands just beyond the Temizusha.
=== Saikan and Anzaisho ===
After passing the first large torii gate, the Purification Hall (Saikan), and the hall for visitors from the imperial household (Anzaisho) is located to the left. The Saikan is used by shrine priests to purify themselves before performing ceremonies at the shrine. They are required to spend one or two nights to free their minds of worldly issues, partaking in baths and eating meals cooked with the sacred fire.
=== Kaguraden ===
[[File:IseShrine.jpg|left|thumb|[[Kagura-den]]]]
This hall for special prayer, located just after the second large torii gate, is open to the public for the offering of individual prayers to the kami, the giving of donations and the purchase of special talisman of protection, amulets and hanging scrolls of Amaterasu Omikami.
[[File:Geku_uiho20051116.JPG|right|thumb|Charge field prayer, Toyōke Daijingū (Gekū), 2005.]]
=== Imibiyaden ===
[[File:Kazahinomi-sai01.jpg|left|thumb|Imibiyaden, 2007]]
This hall contains the sacred fire used to cook all of the food offerings to the kami of Ise Shrine. Rice and other offerings cooked on the sacred fire are stored in a box made of Japanese cypress, then purified at the Haraedo immediately in front of the Imibiyaden before being offered to the kami.
=== Honden ===
The pilgrimage path then approaches the fence of the inner sanctum (昇殿, shōden) of Naikū by a set of large stone steps. Within another set of fencing inside the gate is the main shrine (正宮, seigū) itself. Visitors are supposed to keep to the sides of the path as the middle is set aside for the goddess Amaterasu. Etiquette is the same as for most Shinto shrines. Though the actual shrine is hidden behind a large fence, pilgrims can approach the gate to offer their prayers.  Photographs in this area are prohibited and this restriction is strictly policed.
Kotai Jingū is said to hold the [[Yata no Kagami|Sacred Mirror]], one of three {{ill|Imperial Regalia of Japan|en|Imperial Regalia of Japan|qid=Q327465|lt=Imperial Regalia of Japan|1=Imperial Regalia of Japan}} said to have been given to the first Emperor by the gods.<ref name=":1" /> From a path that follows the line of the outer wall, the distinctive roof of the shrine building can be seen through the trees. In front of the walled shrine compound can be seen an open area which was the location of the rebuilding of the shrine in 2013.
== Sessha ==
=== Naiku Betsugu ===
**Betsugū** (別宮) refers to "wakemiya" (subsidiary shrines) of the **Shōgu** (正宮, Main Shrines), meaning they are considered the most sacred shrines after the Main Shrines within the Ise Grand Shrine complex. There are a total of **10 Betsugū**. <ref>伊勢市観光協会"[http://www.ise-kanko.jp/jingu/betugu.html 伊勢市観光協会/別宮]"（2012nd year 1月8日閲覧。）</ref>

=== Naiku sessha ===
'''Sessha''' (摂社) refers to {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=shrines|1=Shinto shrine}} listed in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki Jinmyōchō|qq=}}, excluding the {{ill|main shrines|ja|正宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/main shrines|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and {{ill|betsugū|ja|別宮|lt=Betsugū|1=Setsumatsusha|2=ja|3=摂末社|4=zh|5=攝末社|6=es|7=Setsumatsusha|8=fr|9=Setsumatsusha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/betsugū|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. By definition, all sessha are considered {{ill|shikinaisha|ja|式内社|1=Shikinaisha|2=ja|3=式内社|1=Shikinaisha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/shikinaisha|13=User:Immanuelle|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyocho|lt=Shikinaisha}}. However, nearly all of them were abolished during the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sengoku period|1=Sengoku Period (Japan)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q117415390}} and were later restored from the {{ill|Kan'ei|en|Kan'ei|qid=Q1192913|lt=Kanei era|1=Kan'ei}} (1630s) through the early {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}} (1870s). As such, they are sometimes identified as the designated locations of shikinaisha.<ref>{{ill|Katsunoshin Sakurai|ja|櫻井勝之進|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsunoshin Sakurai|1=Katsunoshin Sakurai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11544758}} "Ise Jingu" (『{{ill|Ise Shrine|en|Ise Shrine|qid=Q687168|lt=Ise Jingu|1=Ise Grand Shrine}}』)</ref> In total, there are 27 shrines.

=== Naiku Massha ===

=== Naiku Shakansha ===
The term "所管社" (Shokansha) refers to shrines that are not classified as main shrines (正宮, Shōgū), auxiliary shrines (別宮, Betsugū), associated shrines (摂社, Sessha), or subordinate shrines (末社, Massha). In the context of the Ise Grand Shrine (伊勢神宮, Ise Jingū), there are 30 such shrines. 16 of Kotai Jingu and 14 of Toyouke Jingu

== Shrine Animals ==
=== Sacred Roosters ===
[[File:Shinkei, messenger of Amaterasu.jpg|thumb|Sacred Roosters]]
Within the shrine grounds, roosters are kept freely as messengers of the gods. They are considered divine messengers because it is said that a rooster crowed when Amaterasu Ōmikami emerged from the cave, signaling the rise of the sun.
The Jingu Dedicated Rooster Preservation Society, formed by poultry enthusiasts from eight prefectures including Mie, offers sacred roosters to Naiku.<ref name="cn20110606">Ōtsuki Miyako, "Ise Jingu Naiku: Dedication of Oguni Chickens and Others by Poultry Enthusiasts from Eight Prefectures," Chūnichi Shimbun, June 6, 2011, Shima-Muro Regional Edition, p.16.</ref> During the dedication ceremony on June 5, 2011, two pairs (four birds) of Oguni chickens, along with 25 other birds, including {{ill|Japanese Bantam|ja|チャボ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Bantam|1=Q11318153|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11318153}} and {{ill|Onagadori|en|Onagadori|qid=Q730956|lt=Onagadori|1=Onagadori}}, were released within the shrine grounds.<ref name="sk"/> These sacred roosters roost in trees at night.<ref>Shufu no Tomosha (2011), p.30.</ref>
During the various rituals of the {{ill|Jingū Shikinen Sengū|lt=Jingū Shikinen Sengū|lt=Shikinen Sengu|ja|式年遷宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shikinen Sengu|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 遷宮}}, 22 pairs (44 birds) of roosters serve as divine messengers.<ref name="sm1">Yano (2006), p.29.</ref> In the Sengu ceremonies, the selected roosters must have an elegant appearance, a fine crow, be in excellent health, remain calm and dignified during the rituals, and have the longest tails possible among purebred Japanese chickens.<ref name="sm1"/> During each festival, a pair of roosters is placed inside a bamboo cage as "Ikimitsuki" (living offerings) and, after the festival concludes, they are released into the shrine gardens.<ref>Yano (2006), pp.29-30.</ref>
=== Sacred Horses ===
[[File:Soraisamugo -Shinme, God Horse.jpg|thumb|Sacred Horse "Soraisamugo"]]
At Naiku, two sacred horses offered by the imperial family are kept.<ref name="jp">JTB Publishing (2011), p.140.</ref> They are sometimes housed in the stables (御厩, Miumaya), but depending on the weather and their condition, they may not always be present.<ref>Publishing Business Headquarters Domestic Information Division Third Editorial Department (2014), p.17.</ref> Locals respectfully refer to them as "Ouma-sama" (honorific for horses). Though they remain composed even when photographed,<ref>Shufu no Tomosha (2011), pp.24, 81, 87.</ref> flash photography is prohibited.
On the 1st, 11th, and 21st of each month, a ritual known as "Shinme Kenzan" (神馬牽参) is performed, where the sacred horse is led to the main shrine for worship.<ref name="jp"/> Around 8 AM, accompanied by shrine priests, the sacred horse proceeds to the main shrine and bows before the stone steps of the sanctuary.<ref>Shufu no Tomosha (2011), p.87.</ref> During the ceremony, the horse wears a ceremonial robe adorned with the {{ill|Chrysanthemum Seal|ja|菊花紋章|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chrysanthemum Seal|1=Kikumon (chrysanthemum crests)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11082563}}.<ref name="jp"/>
Similarly, at Geku, two sacred horses are kept, and they perform the same Shinme Kenzan ritual on the same days.<ref name="jp"/>
== Local Information ==
[[File:Ise Shrine Naiku area Aerial photograph.1983.jpg|thumb|270px|Aerial photograph of the Naikū area, taken in 1983.<br/>{{National Land Aerial Photograph}}.]]
; **Location**
* {{flag|Mie Prefecture}}<br>[[File:Flag_of_Ise,_Mie.svg|border|25px]] {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|qid=Q328067|lt=Ise City|1=Ise, Mie}}, Ujitachicho 1
; **Transportation Access**
{{underline|Railway}}
* Nearest Station: {{ill|Kintetsu Railway|en|Kintetsu Railway|qid=Q1531085|lt=Kintetsu|1=Kintetsu Railway}} [[:en:Kintetsu Toba Line|Toba Line]] {{ill|Isuzugawa Station|en|Isuzugawa Station|qid=Q6089533|lt=Isuzugawa Station|1=Isuzugawa Station}}
** **Walking:** Approximately 30 minutes
** **Bus:** Approximately 10 minutes (routes from Ujiyamada Station, Ise City Station, and Gekū)
* Kintetsu [[:en:Kintetsu Yamada Line|Yamada Line]]・Toba Line {{ill|Ujiyamada Station|en|Ujiyamada Station|qid=Q7878210|lt=Ujiyamada Station|1=Ujiyamada Station}}
** **Bus:** Approximately 15 minutes
* {{ill|Central Japan Railway Company|en|Central Japan Railway Company|qid=Q513679|lt=JR Central|1=Central Japan Railway Company}} {{ill|Sangū Line|en|Sangū Line|qid=Q872023|lt=Sangū Line|1=Sangū Line}}・Kintetsu Yamada Line [[Ise City Station]]
** **Bus:** Approximately 15 minutes
{{underline|By Car}}
* From {{ill|Ise Expressway|en|Ise Expressway|qid=Q6079578|lt=Ise Expressway|1=Ise Expressway}} [[Ise Nishi Interchange|Ise Nishi IC]], take [[Mie Prefectural Route 32]] (Mikimoto Road) south, then turn south at the "Urata" intersection onto the [[Ise Sangu Kaidō|Ise Kaidō]].
* **Parking:** Use the visitor parking lots near Uji Bridge.
** During peak congestion, private vehicles are restricted from entering the Naikū area from the Urata Town intersection. Visitors are advised to use the **Ise City Municipal Parking Lot** in Uji Urata Town or the parking facilities at **Mie Kōtsū G Sports no Mori Ise** (Mie Prefectural General Sports Complex, Isuzu Park) (paid parking).
** During the **Hatsumōde** period, starting from midnight on **New Year's Eve** and continuing for several days including the **first three days of January**, a **park-and-ride system** is implemented using the **Mie Prefectural Sun Arena** parking lot and **bus-exclusive lanes** (in effect since **2003**). A similar **park-and-ride** system is also implemented during **Golden Week** (**as of 2010**).
